headings.title: Introduction to Body Cavities
headings.content: Body cavities are internal spaces within the human body that protect, separate, and support internal organs. They are broadly divided into two main groups based on their embryonic development and location: the dorsal cavity located at the back of the body, and the ventral cavity located at the front. These fluid-filled spaces cushion delicate organs against physical shocks from walking, jumping, or accidental trauma.

headings.title: Dorsal Body Cavity: Cranial and Spinal Regions
headings.content:
The dorsal body cavity sits posteriorly and houses the structures of the central nervous system. It is subdivided into two continuous regions:
- **Cranial cavity**: Formed by the skull bones, it encloses, protects, and supports the brain.
- **Spinal cavity**: Formed by the vertebrae of the spine, it runs through the vertebral column to enclose and protect the spinal cord.

headings.title: Ventral Body Cavity and Thoracic Subdivisions
headings.content: The ventral cavity is the larger anterior cavity of the body. A major muscular partition called the diaphragm separates it into an upper thoracic cavity and a lower abdominopelvic cavity. The thoracic cavity is further enclosed by the rib cage and contains the heart, lungs, great vessels, and esophagus. It is divided into smaller compartments: the pleural cavities around the lungs and the pericardial cavity enclosing the heart.

headings.title: Abdominopelvic Cavity Organization
headings.content:
The abdominopelvic cavity spans from the diaphragm down to the floor of the pelvis. Although it is a continuous physical space, healthcare providers divide it conceptually into two parts:
- **Abdominal cavity**: Contains digestive organs such as the stomach, intestines, liver, spleen, and kidneys.
- **Pelvic cavity**: Contains the urinary bladder, reproductive organs, and the rectum.

To communicate clearly during patient assessments, nurses use a grid of four abdominal quadrants (right upper, left upper, right lower, left lower) or nine smaller regions.

headings.title: Serous Membranes of the Ventral Cavity
headings.content:
The walls of the ventral body cavity and the outer surfaces of internal organs are covered by a thin, slippery double-layered membrane called the serous membrane. 
- **Parietal layer**: The part of the membrane that lines the walls of the cavity itself.
- **Visceral layer**: The inner part that folds inward to cover the surface of the organs.

A lubricating serous fluid produced by these layers reduces friction as organs move, such as when the lungs expand or the heart beats.

headings.title: Clinical Significance in Nursing Assessment
headings.content: Understanding body cavities guides physical examination and clinical reasoning. When a patient reports pain, knowing which cavity and quadrant the discomfort originates from points the nurse toward specific underlying structures. Conditions like peritonitis, pleurisy, or increased intracranial pressure involve inflammation or pressure changes within these closed spaces, requiring prompt recognition and intervention.
